historical_timeline.summary: Born enslaved in Holly Springs, Mississippi.
Both parents and an infant brother died in the yellow fever epidemic; at 16 she took charge of her siblings.
Married Ferdinand L. Barnett in Chicago.
Signed the call for the conference that led to the NAACP.
Ran for the Illinois State Senate.
Died in Chicago after a brief illness, of kidney disease (uremia), at 68.

claims.statement: Ida B. Wells was born enslaved on July 16, 1862, in Holly Springs, Mississippi, during the Civil War.
In the yellow fever epidemic of 1878, when she was 16, both her parents and an infant brother died; she left school and took on the care of her surviving younger siblings, teaching to support them.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the family history and the early loss and responsibility in her social history. The causes of death are as the sources give them.

claims.statement: She was an investigative journalist and editor who documented lynching in the United States, notably in A Red Record (1895), and campaigned against it for the rest of her life; she was also a suffragist and civil rights leader.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors her occupation and her habit of checking every figure for herself in the modern social history.

claims.statement: On June 27, 1895, she married the Chicago attorney Ferdinand L. Barnett, kept her own name alongside his, and settled in Chicago; they had four children.

source_links.locator: four children; kept her maiden name

claims.statement: She signed the call for the 1909 conference that led to the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People and is considered one of its founders, though she was left off the list of its founding committee and later drew away from it.
In 1930 she ran, unsuccessfully, for the Illinois State Senate.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors her continued public work in the year before the modern episode's true-frame dates.

claims.statement: She began writing her autobiography in her last years; it was published after her death as Crusade for Justice: The Autobiography of Ida B. Wells, edited by her youngest daughter, Alfreda M. Duster.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the memoir she is writing in the modern social history.

claims.statement: She died in Chicago on March 25, 1931, at 68, after a brief illness; the cause is given as kidney disease or uremia (uremic poisoning).
claims.clinical_interpretation: History after the modern episode. The anchor for the modern kidney episode: uremia means kidney failure. Sources differ on the day of death (see the editorial resolutions).

source_links.locator: after a brief illness, March 25, 1931 (gives her age as sixty-nine)
died of kidney disease on March 25, 1931 in Chicago

claims.statement: Whether she had chronic kidney disease before her final illness, and what caused her kidney failure, is not recorded in any source consulted; a short final illness ending in uremia is compatible with acute kidney failure, with chronic kidney disease made worse by an acute illness, or with long-standing kidney disease that had not been recognized.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation only. The chronic kidney disease, high blood pressure and every finding in the modern episode are synthetic; the modern episode shows kidney disease found in time, not a claim about her real kidneys.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Chronic kidney disease found in time in a 68-year-old Black woman, a journalist and civic leader in Chicago, who comes in tired with swollen ankles. The teaching contrast is her documented death from kidney failure after a brief illness: here the disease is found, staged and treated years before kidney failure. The episode covers the race-free CKD-EPI 2021 equations (creatinine, then creatinine with cystatin C) and the history of race-based eGFR delaying the recognition and referral of Black patients, as the NKF-ASN Task Force described; staging on the KDIGO 2024 heat map with the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and the kidney failure risk equation; finding the cause (home blood pressure, diabetes screening, urinalysis, kidney ultrasound, and a monoclonal protein screen); APOL1 genetic testing offered with counseling and left to her choice; an ARB and an SGLT2 inhibitor with potassium and creatinine checks; blood pressure control; a statin; stopping naproxen; anemia and mineral and bone checks; vaccinations; a nephrology consultation; and shared decisions about kidney replacement options should the disease progress, under the KDIGO 2024 guideline, the 2025 AHA/ACC blood pressure guideline and the CMID chronic kidney disease monograph.

hpi.narrative: Mrs. Wells returns two weeks after her first visit with her home blood pressure log and the outside report she obtained: two years ago another clinic measured her creatinine at 1.05 mg/dL and reported an eGFR of 64 as normal. That report used an older equation that raised the estimate for Black patients; recalculated with the race-free CKD-EPI 2021 equation it is 59, already reduced, and no urine albumin test was done then. Her home readings over seven days average 150/88. She stopped naproxen at the first visit and uses acetaminophen for her knees, which works. Her ankles still swell a little by evening and she is still tired in the afternoons. She had her kidney ultrasound this morning and saw Dr. Lindqvist-Moore of nephrology afterwards. She asked to see each calculation and was given copies.

assessment_plan.assessment: Confirmed and staged. Race-free eGFR 40 by creatinine and 38 by creatinine with cystatin C, with the earlier value of 59 two years ago showing the disease has been present for at least that long and has fallen by about 10 a year, which is rapid. The older race-adjusted equation would read today's creatinine as 44 and the earlier one as a normal 64; the race-free result recognizes her disease earlier, as the NKF-ASN Task Force intended. Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 228 mg/g on repeat (240 at intake): A2. Urinalysis from the first visit: 1+ protein, no blood, bland sediment. No monoclonal protein; free light chain ratio normal. Hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C antibody and HIV negative; hepatitis B surface antibody negative. Ultrasound today: kidneys 9.6 and 9.4 cm, both echogenic with thin cortex, no obstruction or stones. Kidney failure risk about 7% at 5 years and 2% at 2 years. Dr. Lindqvist-Moore judges hypertensive kidney disease most likely, with APOL1-associated disease possible
plan: Losartan 50 mg daily; potassium and creatinine in two weeks
Dapagliflozin to follow once potassium and creatinine are stable
Kidney education session and a dietitian session
APOL1 testing offered after counseling; she chose to defer it

referral.question: New chronic kidney disease, probably G3b A2, of uncertain cause in a 68-year-old Black woman with tiredness, ankle swelling and high blood pressure readings: race-free eGFR 40 by creatinine and 38 with cystatin C, and a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio of 240 mg/g. Please advise on the cause and further evaluation, APOL1 genetic testing, kidney-protective treatment and its order, the anemia and mineral findings, and how and when to plan for the future
referral.urgency: Within two weeks, on the day of her two-week visit, after the repeat urine test and the kidney ultrasound
referral.pertinent_history: Mrs. Wells is a journalist and civic leader, active and independent, who has been tired for some months and notices ankle swelling by evening. She has taken over-the-counter naproxen for knee aching for about a year; it was stopped today. She has no diabetes symptoms, no known kidney disease, and no blood in the urine. She recalls being told by another clinic two years ago that a kidney test was normal and is obtaining that report. Her parents and an infant brother died in an epidemic in her youth; no family kidney history is known. Blood pressure 164/94 (average of two readings), pulse 78, weight 70.4 kg, BMI 28.6; trace ankle swelling. Results today: sodium 139, potassium 4.6, bicarbonate 22 mmol/L; urea nitrogen 28, creatinine 1.42 mg/dL; eGFR 40 (CKD-EPI 2021 creatinine, race-free); cystatin C 1.68 mg/L, eGFR 38 (creatinine and cystatin C); urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 240 mg/g; fasting glucose 94 mg/dL and A1c 5.6%; hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, ferritin 168 ng/mL, transferrin saturation 24%; calcium 9.2, phosphate 3.8 mg/dL; intact PTH 84 pg/mL; 25-hydroxyvitamin D 17 ng/mL; LDL 136 mg/dL; TSH 1.9; PHQ-9 4. ECG: sinus rhythm with voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy. Sent today: urinalysis with microscopy, serum protein electrophoresis with free light chains, hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV tests. Planned: a home blood pressure monitor for seven days, a repeat urine albumin test and a kidney ultrasound on the morning of your visit. She asks to see every result and how each was calculated
questions: What is the most likely cause of her kidney disease, and does she need further tests, including a kidney biopsy?
Do you agree with the race-free staging, and how should we use cystatin C from here?
Should she be offered APOL1 genetic testing, and how would a result change her care?
Which kidney-protective medicines do you advise, in what order, and with what blood pressure target?
How should we manage the mild anemia, the low vitamin D and the raised PTH?
How often should she be seen by nephrology, and when should planning for kidney replacement begin?

consultant_note.history: Mrs. Wells, 68, is seen at the request of Dr. Ashworth-Banks for chronic kidney disease found two weeks ago. She has been tired for some months and has had ankle swelling by evening. She took naproxen for knee aching for about a year and stopped it two weeks ago. She has no diabetes, no visible blood in the urine, no foamy urine, no rash, joint swelling or mouth ulcers, and no history of kidney stones or urinary infections. She brought an outside report from two years ago: creatinine 1.05 mg/dL with an eGFR of 64 reported as normal, from an equation with a race coefficient. Her home blood pressure average over seven days is 150/88. She asked detailed questions and wants the evidence behind each recommendation
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Intake results as listed by Dr. Ashworth-Banks. Recalculated earlier value: eGFR 59 by the race-free CKD-EPI 2021 equation (64 by the older race-based equation). Today's results by the older equation would read 44. Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 228 mg/g today (240 at intake). Urinalysis: 1+ protein, no blood, no casts; bland sediment. Serum protein electrophoresis: no monoclonal protein; free light chain ratio 1.2, normal for her eGFR. Hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C antibody and HIV negative; hepatitis B surface antibody negative. Kidney ultrasound this morning: right kidney 9.6 cm, left 9.4 cm, both echogenic with thinned cortex, no hydronephrosis, stones or masses. ECG with voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy. Kidney failure risk equation: about 7% at 5 years, 2% at 2 years

exam.finding: Blood pressure 154/90 and pulse 76, measured in clinic today
Regular rhythm; no rub; trace ankle swelling
No rash; no joint swelling

assessment.assessment: Chronic kidney disease G3b A2, present for at least two years and falling by about 10 mL/min a year. The bland urine, moderate albuminuria, small echogenic kidneys and left ventricular hypertrophy point to hypertensive kidney disease; APOL1-associated kidney disease is possible in a woman of African ancestry with this picture. There is no sign of diabetic, glomerular inflammatory or monoclonal disease, and naproxen may have added to the decline. A biopsy is not indicated now; it would be if blood appeared in the urine, albuminuria rose toward the nephrotic range, or eGFR fell quickly despite treatment. The race-free staging is correct: the older equation would have read the earlier result as normal and delayed recognition, which is the harm the NKF-ASN Task Force recommendation was written to end. Use creatinine for routine monitoring and add cystatin C when a decision depends on accuracy, such as drug dosing or transplant evaluation

Stage 2 hypertension, confirmed at home, with target organ damage. An ARB is the foundation with this albuminuria. Goal below 130/80, and a systolic below 120 by standardized measurement if she tolerates it without dizziness
Mild and iron replete; no erythropoiesis-stimulating agent is indicated. Recheck in three months

recommendations: Losartan 50 mg daily now, with potassium and creatinine in two weeks; accept a creatinine rise of up to 30%

Then dapagliflozin 10 mg daily, which KDIGO recommends at her eGFR with albuminuria of 200 mg/g or more, with a further check at two to four weeks; then increase losartan to 100 mg if potassium stays below 5.5 mmol/L. Finerenone is not indicated without diabetes
Sick-day rules in writing: hold losartan and dapagliflozin on days of vomiting, diarrhea or not eating, and before surgery or contrast
No NSAIDs; acetaminophen for knee pain
Atorvastatin 20 mg daily, as KDIGO advises for adults 50 or older with eGFR below 60
Vitamin D3 1,000 units daily; PTH, vitamin D and hemoglobin in three months
Hepatitis B vaccination, since she is not immune, with the other vaccines her primary clinician has planned

APOL1 testing offered after counseling: a result would not change her medicines or blood pressure target now, may inform her risk and any future transplant evaluation, and has implications for relatives; the federal genetic nondiscrimination law does not cover life or long-term care insurance. She chose to defer, and may ask at any time

consultant_note.follow_up: Nephrology review in three months with the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, then every three to six months while eGFR is below 45 and falling. Transplant evaluation and discussion of dialysis access or conservative care when eGFR approaches 20 or the 2-year kidney failure risk passes 10%, earlier if she wishes. Sooner for potassium above 5.5 mmol/L, a fall in eGFR of more than 30% after starting medicines, or blood in the urine. Dr. Ashworth-Banks continues primary care and monitoring
